name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,344

entries.clue: Chief received energy charges (4)

indicatorNotes.charges: To charge a glass or a battery is to load something into it, so one piece goes inside the other.

blocks.note: received = HAD, the past tense serving as the outer word
e = energy, the physicist's symbol

annotation.surface: A boss lands the bill for the electricity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as a noun, the sums on the bill, and works as a verb instead. A battery charged is a battery filled, which is the sense the setter wants.
annotation.definitionFit: The head of a firm or a school is its chief, both nouns for the person in charge.

entries.clue: Conspicuous men — ten I suspect (7)

indicatorNotes.suspect: Calling a thing suspect says it cannot be trusted as it stands, and letters you cannot trust will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: The speaker has doubts about ten of the men on show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conspicuous men' reads as one phrase, which is the trap: only the first word defines, and the second opens the mixture. Eminent is standing out by rank or reputation.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone eminent stands out from those around them, so 'conspicuous' is being used of standing in the world rather than of being easy to spot.

entries.clue: Remain at first diligent and agreeable (5)

indicatorNotes.at first: 'At first' asks how a word starts, and what a word starts with is its opening letter.

blocks.note: the opening letter of diligent
well in the sense of satisfactory, as in 'that sits well with me'

annotation.surface: A new recruit who starts out hard-working and pleasant with it.
annotation.walkthrough: To dwell on a subject is to stay with it past the point of need, and to dwell somewhere is to live there. Both are the staying sense the definition wants.
annotation.definitionFit: To dwell in a place is to remain in it, and both verbs take the same shape in a sentence about staying put.

entries.clue: Men dance in uncle’s premises (8)

blocks.note: the chessmen of the front rank are pawns
a hop is a dance, the village-hall sort

annotation.surface: Men having a dance round at someone's uncle's place.
annotation.walkthrough: Uncle has been slang for a pawnbroker since Georgian times — the man you took the watch to on Monday and redeemed it from on Friday. 'Men' belongs on the chessboard.
annotation.definitionFit: Since 'uncle' is the old slang for a pawnbroker, the premises he keeps are the shop where goods are pledged for cash.

entries.clue: Writer’s verse abridged (3)

indicatorNotes.abridged: An abridged text is cut shorter than it was written, so the word loses its ending.

blocks.note: a poem is a piece of verse

annotation.surface: An author's poetry, printed in a shortened edition.
annotation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe wrote 'The Raven' and the first detective stories, and his name hides inside the very word for what he wrote.
annotation.definitionFit: Poe is Edgar Allan Poe, the American of the tales of terror, so 'Writer' names him by the trade he lived by.

entries.clue: State is on top of those against cracking victory (9)

indicatorNotes.on top of: In a down answer the piece sitting on top of another is written above it, so this one comes first.
indicatorNotes.cracking: Cracking a thing splits it open, so the word named breaks apart to take the rest between its halves.

blocks.note: a victory is a win, and it opens after its first letter
the word itself, taken as two letters
the cons are the arguments against, as in pros and cons

annotation.surface: The people opposed are riding high on the back of a splendid win.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracking victory' is the surface's praise, a terrific win, and underneath it is an instruction to break the word apart. Wisconsin is the dairy state on Lake Michigan's western shore.
annotation.definitionFit: Wisconsin is one of the fifty United States, so 'State' names it by the class it belongs to rather than by synonym.

entries.clue: Pupil finally performs choral works (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: 'Finally' points at how the word beside it ends, so only its last letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.works: Working a material is kneading it into another shape, and letters worked come out in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: the last letter of performs
anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A pupil rounds off the concert with some choral singing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Choral works' is a real category — anthems, oratorios, the Messiah — so the second word reads as a noun and is really the instruction. A scholar can also be a prize pupil holding a scholarship.
annotation.definitionFit: A scholar is a pupil at school, the word surviving in 'head scholar' and in the scholarships that pay for the place.

entries.clue: Flower shows using helpers, essentially around forty (5)

indicatorNotes.essentially: The essence of a word is what sits at its centre, so each word named gives up its middle letter alone.
indicatorNotes.around: Going around a thing is closing over it, so the letters gathered first sit either side of what follows.

blocks.note: the central letters of shOws, usIng and helPers, in that order
XL is forty in Roman numerals, ten short of L

annotation.surface: Flower shows run on volunteers, most of them around forty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower shows' looks like one phrase and the definition stops at the first word. An oxlip is a pale yellow spring wildflower, Shakespeare's 'bold oxlips' in the Midsummer Night's Dream bank.
annotation.definitionFit: The oxlip is a primrose-family wildflower of damp woodland, so 'Flower' names it by class.

entries.clue: Eternal smile set to change (8)

indicatorNotes.to change: Something put to change does not come out as it went in, so its letters take a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A fixed smile that is about to give way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set' reads as an adjective on the surface — a set smile is a stiff one — and it is the back half of the fodder. Timeless means untouched by time, not merely long-lived.
annotation.definitionFit: A timeless style is one the years never date, which is what 'eternal' claims: both adjectives say time has no hold.

entries.clue: Reserved husband joins tea lady off and on (4)

indicatorNotes.off and on: Doing a thing off and on is doing it at intervals rather than throughout, so letters are picked every other one.

blocks.note: h = husband, the standard abbreviation
the second, fourth and sixth letters of tEaLaDy

annotation.surface: A husband turns up now and then to help the tea lady.
annotation.walkthrough: A tea lady is the woman who wheeled the trolley round a British office, once a fixture of the working day. 'Reserved' is the booking sense, a table kept back for you.
annotation.definitionFit: A seat held for you is a seat reserved, the same past participle of keeping something back for one person.

entries.clue: Male with case of laryngeal pain (4)

indicatorNotes.case of: A case is the shell a thing travels in, so what is wanted is the outside of the word and not its contents.

blocks.note: the male pronoun
the first and last letters of laryngeal

annotation.surface: A man laid up with a sore throat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Laryngeal pain' reads as one medical complaint, which hides the join: the last word alone is the definition and the one before it keeps only its case.
annotation.definitionFit: A thing that gives you hell gives you sustained pain, the colloquial noun rather than the underworld.

entries.clue: Online pest pretty much exposed novelist (8)

indicatorNotes.pretty much: 'Pretty much' is not quite all of it, so the word it governs arrives a letter short.

blocks.note: a troll is the poster who baits strangers for sport
exposed = OPEN, stopping one letter early

annotation.surface: An internet nuisance all but unmasked.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is thoroughly modern and the answer thoroughly Victorian, which is the clue's joke. Trollope also worked for the Post Office and gave Britain the pillar box.
annotation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope wrote the Barchester and Palliser sequences, so 'novelist' names him by the trade.

entries.clue: Tense philosopher’s articles collected by bride (9)

blocks.note: t = tense, as grammar books mark it
Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the Geneva-born philosopher of the social contract

annotation.surface: A jumpy philosopher whose papers a bride has been gathering up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' pulls towards a philosopher's published papers and means clothes and linen instead. Trousseau is French for a little bundle, which is what the bride packs.
annotation.definitionFit: A trousseau is exactly the clothes and linen a bride assembles for her marriage, so the definition describes the thing rather than naming a synonym.

entries.clue: Trims back half of corn plaster (6)

indicatorNotes.back: Sent back, a word is written out from its last letter to its first.
indicatorNotes.half of: Half of a word stops at its midpoint, keeping the opening letters and dropping the rest.

blocks.note: trims = CUTS, then written backwards
the front half of CORN

annotation.surface: Cutting a corn plaster down by half before sticking it on.
annotation.walkthrough: A corn plaster is the padded dressing you put on a foot corn, and the surface leans on that whole phrase. Only the last word is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Stucco is the fine plaster rendering spread over the outside of a building, so 'plaster' names the material it is.

entries.clue: Cocaine from Chile distributed round centres in far north (7)

indicatorNotes.distributed: Distributing something hands it out afresh, so the letters are dealt into another order.
indicatorNotes.round: Going round a thing puts it inside, so the dealt letters close over the pair that follows.
indicatorNotes.centres in: The centre of a word is its middle letter, and each word named gives up that letter only.

blocks.note: the letters of CHILE dealt again, then opened to take the insert
the middle letters of fAr and noRth

annotation.surface: Cocaine shipped out of Chile is doing the rounds up in the far north.
annotation.walkthrough: Charlie is British street slang for cocaine, taken from the drug's initial letter. 'Far north' looks like the destination of the shipment and supplies two letters from the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Charlie has been street slang for cocaine for decades, a nickname off the C that the police alphabet turns into a name.

entries.clue: Gutted Scrooge stifles copy writer (6)

indicatorNotes.Gutted: Gutting takes out the insides, so a word keeps its first and last letters and nothing between.
indicatorNotes.stifles: To stifle a thing is to smother it, holding it inside, so what is left closes over the piece named next.

blocks.note: SCROOGE emptied of everything between its S and its E
to crib is to copy someone else's work

annotation.surface: A devastated Scrooge smothering the man who writes his copy.
annotation.walkthrough: Gutted is British for bitterly disappointed, which is the surface sense, while the wordplay wants the butcher's. 'Copy writer' splits, the first word into the wordplay and the second into the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A scribe is a copyist of documents, the clerk who writes things out, so 'writer' is the plain job description.

entries.clue: Lazy sort upset house, beginning to insult ballet company (7)

indicatorNotes.upset: Upset means tipped over, and in a down answer a tipped word reads upwards instead of down.
indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, and that is all this takes.

blocks.note: a lazy sort is a SLOB, turned upwards
ho = house, as an address is abbreviated
the opening letter of insult

annotation.surface: A layabout upsets the household and starts hurling abuse at the dancers.
annotation.walkthrough: Bolshoi is simply Russian for big, and the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow took its name from its size. 'Upset' pays twice: the surface's annoyance, the grid's turnaround.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bolshoi is the Moscow ballet company housed at the Bolshoi Theatre, so the definition names the institution itself.

entries.clue: Murderer, fiend, regularly pursues two nincompoops (8)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly come at an even beat, every other one, with the rest left behind.
indicatorNotes.pursues: To pursue is to come along behind, so these letters take their place after the ones already down.

blocks.note: an ass is a nincompoop, and this is the first of the pair
the second one, written straight after the first
the even-placed letters of fIeNd

annotation.surface: A killer and a brute who makes a habit of going after a couple of fools.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Murderer, fiend' reads as one description of the same man, and only the first word defines. Ass here is the donkey sense of fool, the one British English has always used.
annotation.definitionFit: An assassin kills a chosen victim, usually a public figure, so 'murderer' is the general word for what the answer does to order.

entries.clue: Stigma of Communist leader abandoning Left (5)

indicatorNotes.abandoning: What a word abandons it no longer carries, so the letter named drops out of it.

blocks.note: Stalin ran the Soviet Communist Party for thirty years
l = left, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A Communist boss walking out on the political Left.
annotation.walkthrough: Capitalising 'Left' makes it political, in keeping with the surface, while it works as a one-letter abbreviation. The mark meant here is on a reputation, not on a shirt.
annotation.definitionFit: A stain on someone's name is the mark of disgrace they carry about with them, which is what a stigma is.

entries.clue: Notify small group of intellectuals (4)

indicatorNotes.small group of: A small group of a word is a short run of its letters, taken from inside rather than the whole.

blocks.note: inTELLectuals carries it, starting at the third letter

annotation.surface: Letting a little circle of thinkers in on the news.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small group of intellectuals' sounds like a definition in its own right — a think tank, an elite — and is really an instruction about how much of the last word to take.
annotation.definitionFit: To tell someone something is to notify them of it, the same verb in an everyday register instead of an official one.

entries.clue: Idiot suppresses second wind (5)

indicatorNotes.suppresses: To suppress a thing is to hold it down inside you, so the letter named sits within the word before it.

blocks.note: a twit is an idiot, and the word opens before its last letter
s = second, as a stopwatch marks it

annotation.surface: A fool smothering the second wind that would have kept him going.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second wind' is the runner's revival and reads as one phrase, but the two words belong on opposite sides of the clue. The wind of the definition rhymes with 'find'.
annotation.definitionFit: To twist a wire round a post is to wind it round, the verb of coiling rather than the noun for a breeze.

entries.clue: Incredible time, everything coming together (4)

indicatorNotes.coming together: Two things coming together are set side by side, so the pieces are written one straight after the other.

blocks.note: t = time, the letter physics gives it in a formula
everything is all

annotation.surface: A wonderful evening on which everything falls into place at once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Incredible time' reads as one phrase, a great night out, and the split falls between the two words. A tall story is one too big to swallow.
annotation.definitionFit: A tall order or a tall tale is one beyond belief, so 'Incredible' is the exaggeration sense of the word and has nothing to do with height.

entries.clue: View agreement rowing crew accepts (8)

indicatorNotes.accepts: A crew that accepts something takes it aboard, so the piece named goes inside the other.

blocks.note: an eight is the eight-oared crew of a racing boat, and it opens after its first letter
a yes is the word of agreement

annotation.surface: Looking over the terms the rowing crew are prepared to accept.
annotation.walkthrough: 'View agreement' opens the clue as though it were an instruction to read a contract, and the first word is a noun standing alone. In rowing an eight is the boat and the crew in it.
annotation.definitionFit: Eyesight is the power of seeing, and 'view' carries that sense in 'in plain view' — what the eye can take in.

entries.clue: Animal solvers caught (3)

indicatorNotes.caught: Catching what someone says is hearing it, so the word is taken by its sound and not its spelling.

blocks.note: the solvers are the ones reading it, that is 'you', and said aloud that is the sheep

annotation.surface: The people doing the puzzle have caught an animal.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue turns and speaks to whoever is reading it, which is where the sound comes from. Three letters is often a sign the wordplay will be this direct.
annotation.definitionFit: A ewe is a female sheep, so 'Animal' names it by the widest class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Shaky cushy job having start delayed (8)

indicatorNotes.having start delayed: Delaying the start holds the opening letter back so that it arrives further into the word, the others closing up ahead of it.

blocks.note: a sinecure is a post that pays a salary and asks no work

annotation.surface: A comfortable post whose starting date keeps being put back.
annotation.walkthrough: Sinecure is Latin for 'without care', an office with a stipend and no duties attached. Only its opening letter travels; every other letter stays where it was.
annotation.definitionFit: Something insecure is not firmly fixed — an insecure ladder, an insecure position — so 'Shaky' is the same adjective of instability.

entries.clue: People in line humiliated, partly taken aback (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is plural where the answer is singular, because the answer is the collective noun for the body of people the definition describes.

indicatorNotes.partly: Only part of what follows is wanted, so the letters sit as a run inside the word rather than making it up.
indicatorNotes.taken aback: Taken aback is knocked backwards, so the run is read from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: humiLIATed holds LIAT, and that read backwards gives the answer

annotation.surface: People queueing, shamed and a little startled by it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Humiliated, partly' looks like a description of the people, and the comma covers the join. The run hides inside a single word and runs the wrong way, which is why it sits so quietly.
annotation.definitionFit: A tail is the string of people trailing behind at the back of a queue, the line itself seen from its far end.
